title: Cap. XII: Tranfit vers. XIX — Constituti peccatores; Chamier causaliter
pass_a_gloss: That learned man passes over to verse 19. And from it he argues thus. We were constituted sinners through Adam's disobedience; therefore it was imputed to us. By means of hereditary corruption, I grant; immediately, I deny. He seems to want to prove the consequence. For who, I ask, he says, could that κατάστασις, that ἁμαρτία, that παράπτωμα, constitute us guilty, [or] lead τὸ παράπτωμα of Rom. verse 18 (which indeed is a judicial act, an utterance of God's justice, and its effect—damnation, condemnation) into us apart from actual sin, whether proper or imputed? Away with this delirium. The reply is easy. It can constitute us guilty, as Chamier speaks, causally, by original sin produced and propagated into us. Nor is that delirium; but the Church's constant doctrine, which Scripture and experience attest to be true. How, he adds, be constituted sinners, namely in act, without sin? Which since it cannot be original—inasmuch as that is still only habitual, especially in the newly conceived or born—it remains that it is some actual sin. I answer: we are constituted sinners not without sin: for original sin is truly sin. But it is not [actual] in act. Rather it is in act a habitual sin: in act it inheres in infants: in act it makes us liable to divine wrath. If you deny this, you scarcely differ from Pighius's opinion.
pass_b_english: That learned man moves on to verse 19, and argues from it: we were made sinners by Adam's disobedience, therefore it was imputed to us. Through hereditary corruption—I grant; immediately—I deny. He seems bent on proving the consequence. Who, he asks, could that κατάστασις, that ἁμαρτία, that παράπτωμα make us guilty, or bring the παράπτωμα of Romans 5:18 (a judicial act, God's justice spoken out, and its effect: damnation, condemnation) upon us without actual sin, whether our own or imputed? Away with the delirium. The answer is plain. As Chamier puts it, it can make us guilty causally, by original sin produced and propagated into us. That is no delirium; it is the Church's settled doctrine, which Scripture and experience confirm. How, he adds, can we be constituted sinners in act without sin? Since that cannot be original sin—still only habitual, especially in the newly conceived or newborn—it must be some actual sin. I answer: we are constituted sinners not without sin, for original sin is truly sin. It is not an actual act; it is, in act, habitual sin: in act it inheres in infants; in act it makes us liable to God's wrath. Deny that, and you are scarcely off Pighius's path.
source_text: Tranfit ille Vir doctus ad vers. XIX. Ex eoque sic argumentatur. Constituti sumus peccatores per inobedientiam Adami; Ergo nobis imputata fuit. Mediante corruptione hereditaria, Concedo: Immediate, Nego. Videtur probare velle consequentiam. Nam qui quaeso, inquit, illa κατάστασις, illa ἁμαρτία, illud παράπτωμα, nos potuit reos constituere, τὸ παράπτωμα Rom. vers. 18. (quod quidem est actus judiciarius, justitiae Dei effatum, & effectum, damnatio, condemnatio) in nos inducere citra peccatum actuale, vel proprium, vel imputatum? Apage hoc delirium. Facilis est responsio. Potest nos reos constituere, ut loquitur Chamierus, causaliter, producto & propagato in nos peccato originali. Neque id est delirium; sed constans Ecclesiae doctrina, quam veram esse Scriptura & experientia contestantur. Quomodo, subjungit, constitui peccatores, scilicet actu, sine peccato? Quod cum non possit esse originale, quippe quod tantum adhuc habituale, praesertim in recens conceptis aut natis, superest ut sit quoddam actuale peccatum. Respondeo, constitui peccatores non sine peccato: nam peccatum originale est vere peccatum. At non est actu. Imo est actu peccatum habituale: actu inhaeret infantibus: actu nos facit reos irae divinae. Hoc si negas, a Pighii opinione vix distas.
